newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ expects Iran to withdraw envoy amid trade ban.
newsitem.headline: NZ expects Iran to withdraw envoy amid trade ban.

text.p: A New Zealand official on Monday said Iran may withdraw its ambassador to Wellington in line with action already taken across Europe in a row over a German court ruling that Tehran ordered political killings.
However, government officials said they were not actively seeking confirmation of a report that Iran had imposed a trade ban on New Zealand.
Asked if he expected the Iranian envoy to be withdrawn, senior foreign ministry official John Hayes told Reuters: "I would expect the Iranians to take consistent action across a range of countries."
On Sunday Iran withdrew its ambassadors from all European Union countries, except Greece, after those countries withdrew their envoys for consultations.
New Zealand, Australia and Canada also withdrew their ambassadors.
"Our ambassador will be back for a day or two...," said Hayes, director of the ministry's Middle East and Africa division.

Hayes said Wellington had had no formal advice from any government source of Saturday's report by the official news agency IRNA that Iran had imposed a ban on imports of New Zealand meat, butter and wool, and was seeking other suppliers.

IRNA said the ban was a response New Zealand's move to join international action to recall envoys to Tehran after a German court ruling that Iran ordered the 1992 murders of four Kurdish dissidents in Berlin.
Hayes said he was not aware of any trade bans by Iran on other countries. "Nor are we aware of one on New Zealand".
So far, Wellington had only seen media reports and was not seeking confirmation of the ban, he said.
A spokesman for the Iranian Embassy in Wellington told Reuters no diplomatic staff were available for comment.
New Zealand authorities said Iran was a relatively small market for the country's primary exports, but was nonetheless valuable.
Radio New Zealand quoted some exporters as saying they were concerned that any ban might mean Tehran would halt payments for consignments already delivered to the Gulf.
Last year producer boards sold meat, fish, dairy products and wool worth about NZ$170 million (US$119 million) to Iran, according to trade sources.
